title: Structures as offset tables
summary: Lay out a struct as named field offsets with the padding it needs, read and write each field at its own size, and nest one struct inside another.

body.markdown:
Read these first:

- [Memory: loads, stores, and addressing modes](/learn/memory-and-addressing-modes)
- [Arrays in memory, in one and two dimensions](/learn/arrays-in-memory)

A *structure* (a `struct` in C) groups values of different types under one name, such as a book's year, page count, and shelf letter. Each value in it is a *field*. In memory a struct is one block of bytes, and each field sits at a fixed distance from the start of the block, called its *offset*. Assembly has no struct keyword: you write the offsets down as named numbers and add them to the struct's address.

## Alignment and padding

The fields do not simply follow one another. Each field starts at an offset that is a multiple of its own size: a short on a multiple of 2, an int on a multiple of 4, a long or a pointer on a multiple of 8. A field placed this way is *aligned*. To keep every field aligned, the compiler leaves unused bytes, called *padding*, in front of any field that would otherwise start in the wrong place.

In `struct book`, `year` takes offsets 0 and 1. `pages` cannot start at 2, which is not a multiple of 4, so bytes 2 and 3 are padding and `pages` takes 4 to 7. `shelf` takes byte 8. The whole struct then grows to a multiple of its widest field's size, here 4, so its 9 bytes become 12. That end padding matters in an array of books: every element then starts on a multiple of 4, and so does every `pages` field inside it.

| offset | bytes | holds |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 2 | `year` |
| 2 | 2 | padding |
| 4 | 4 | `pages` |
| 8 | 1 | `shelf` |
| 9 | 3 | padding |

AArch64 can load a word from an address that is not a multiple of 4 in most cases, but C always lays a struct out with this padding. A struct that assembly shares with C code has to match the C layout byte for byte, so the programs here follow the same rules.

## Offsets as names

Write the layout down once, one name per field, and use the names everywhere after that. `book_pages = 4` is an *equate*: it gives the number 4 a name, and the assembler puts 4 wherever `book_pages` appears. With the record's address in `book_r`, the `pages` field is at `[book_r, book_pages]`. If the layout ever changes, only the table of equates changes with it.

## One load size per field

Each field is read and written with the instruction that matches its size:

| field | store | load |
|---|---|---|
| char, 1 byte | `strb` | `ldrb` |
| short, 2 bytes | `strh` | `ldrsh` |
| int, 4 bytes | `str` with a `w` register | `ldr` with a `w` register |
| long or pointer, 8 bytes | `str` with an `x` register | `ldr` with an `x` register |

The wrong width touches the wrong bytes. A 4-byte `str` into `shelf` also writes the three bytes after it, which are padding here but could be the next field in another struct. A 4-byte `ldr` from `year` reads the padding into the top half of the value.

The narrow loads also have to fill the rest of the register. `ldrsh` *sign-extends*: it copies the top bit of the short into every higher bit, so -5 stays -5. `ldrh` fills them with zeros instead, so the same bytes read as 65531. A plain `char` on AArch64 Linux holds 0 to 255, so `shelf` is read with `ldrb`, which fills with zeros.

The program below stores one book in the frame and reads it back. The record needs 12 bytes, so `alloc = -(16 + 12) & -16`, which is -32, and the record starts at `fp + 16`; `add book_r, fp, book_s` puts that address in a register once. That register is `x19`, so the address survives the `printf` calls; like the other short programs before the subroutine lessons, this `main` uses it without saving it first. It prints:

body.source:
a book record takes 12 bytes
year 2019, 412 pages, shelf C

body.starter:
// One book record in the frame: store each field at its offset, then read them back

define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)
define(book_r, x19)

// struct book { short year; int pages; char shelf; }
book_year = 0                               // 2 bytes, then 2 bytes of padding
book_pages = 4                              // an int starts on a multiple of 4
book_shelf = 8                              // 1 byte, then 3 bytes of padding
book_size = 12                              // 9 rounded up to a multiple of 4

book_s = 16                                 // the record starts 16 bytes above fp
alloc = -(16 + book_size) & -16
dealloc = -alloc

.data
fmt_size:   .string "a book record takes %d bytes\n"
fmt_book:   .string "year %d, %d pages, shelf %c\n"

.text
        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, alloc]!
        mov     fp, sp

        add     book_r, fp, book_s          // book_r = address of the record

        mov     w9, 2019
        strh    w9, [book_r, book_year]     // a short takes a 2-byte store
        mov     w9, 412
        str     w9, [book_r, book_pages]    // an int takes a 4-byte store
        mov     w9, 'C'
        strb    w9, [book_r, book_shelf]    // a char takes a 1-byte store

        ldr     x0, =fmt_size
        mov     w1, book_size
        bl      printf

        ldr     x0, =fmt_book
        ldrsh   w1, [book_r, book_year]     // sign-extend: a short can be negative
        ldr     w2, [book_r, book_pages]
        ldrb    w3, [book_r, book_shelf]    // zero-extend: a char code runs 0 to 255
        bl      printf

        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], dealloc
        ret

expectedOutput.stdout:
a book record takes 12 bytes
year 2019, 412 pages, shelf C

body.markdown: Field order changes the size. Put the int first, `{ int pages; short year; char shelf; }`, and the offsets become 0, 4 and 6 with one byte of padding at the end: 8 bytes instead of 12. Try it: set `book_pages = 0`, `book_year = 4`, `book_shelf = 6` and `book_size = 8`. The program prints `a book record takes 8 bytes` and the same three fields.

## A struct inside a struct

A field can itself be a struct. It is aligned by the size of its own widest field, and a field inside it sits at the outer offset plus the inner offset. A library loan can hold two dates:

The month of the due date is at `loan_due + date_month`, which is `8 + 2 = 10`. The assembler adds the two names for you, so `ldrb w5, [loan_r, loan_due + date_month]` is one load with the fixed offset 10. Writing the equates in terms of each other (`loan_due = loan_out + date_size`) means a change to `date` moves every field after it.

The program below records a loan taken out in November 2026 and works out the due date three months later, carrying into the next year when the month passes 12. It prints `book 7031: out 2026/11, due 2027/02`.

body.starter:
// A loan record holding two date records: an inner field sits at outer offset + inner offset

define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)
define(loan_r, x19)

// struct date { short year; char month; }
date_year = 0                               // 2 bytes
date_month = 2                              // 1 byte, then 1 byte of padding
date_size = 4                               // 3 rounded up to a multiple of 2

// struct loan { int id; struct date out; struct date due; }
loan_id = 0                                 // 4 bytes
loan_out = 4                                // a date needs a multiple of 2, and 4 is one
loan_due = loan_out + date_size             // 8
loan_size = loan_due + date_size            // 12

loan_s = 16
alloc = -(16 + loan_size) & -16
dealloc = -alloc

.data
fmt:        .string "book %d: out %d/%02d, due %d/%02d\n"

.text
        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, alloc]!
        mov     fp, sp

        add     loan_r, fp, loan_s          // loan_r = address of the loan

        mov     w9, 7031
        str     w9, [loan_r, loan_id]
        mov     w9, 2026
        strh    w9, [loan_r, loan_out + date_year]
        mov     w9, 11
        strb    w9, [loan_r, loan_out + date_month]

        // due = out + 3 months, carrying into the next year past December
        ldrsh   w10, [loan_r, loan_out + date_year]
        ldrb    w11, [loan_r, loan_out + date_month]
        add     w11, w11, 3
        cmp     w11, 12
        b.le    store_due
        sub     w11, w11, 12
        add     w10, w10, 1
store_due:
        strh    w10, [loan_r, loan_due + date_year]
        strb    w11, [loan_r, loan_due + date_month]

        ldr     x0, =fmt
        ldr     w1, [loan_r, loan_id]
        ldrsh   w2, [loan_r, loan_out + date_year]
        ldrb    w3, [loan_r, loan_out + date_month]
        ldrsh   w4, [loan_r, loan_due + date_year]
        ldrb    w5, [loan_r, loan_due + date_month]
        bl      printf

        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], dealloc
        ret

body.markdown:
## An array of structs

An array of structs puts this lesson and the arrays lesson together. Element `i` starts at `base + i * size_of_struct`, and a field inside it adds the field's offset: the `pages` field of book `i` is at `base + i * 12 + 4`, which is always a multiple of 4 thanks to the end padding. The scaled load from the arrays lesson only multiplies by 1, 2, 4 or 8, so for a 12-byte struct work out `i * 12` with `mul` first and add it to the base.

## Check yourself

1. Give the offsets and the size of `struct s { char c; long n; short h; }`.
2. A short field holds -3. What do `ldrsh` and `ldrh` read from it?
3. In the loan program, what offset does `loan_out + date_month` stand for?
4. An array of five `struct book` starts at `0x3000`. Where is the `shelf` field of element 3?

Answers:

1. `c` at 0, `n` at 8, `h` at 16, and the size is 24, because 18 rounds up to a multiple of 8.
2. -3 and 65533.
3. 6.
4. `0x3000 + 3 * 12 + 8 = 0x302c`.
